extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, economists, and students of political economy; readers concerned with trade policy and public finance
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging mercantile-era trade and governance policies — e.g., monopolies, bounties, prohibitions, and the behavior of chartered companies and their servants — with attention to public revenue, production, and distributional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign interest: increase annual produce
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign's revenue is drawn from that of the people; 'The greater the revenue of the people, therefore, the greater the annual produce of their land and labour... It is his interest, therefore, to increase as much as possible that annual produce.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should be judged by whether it increases the annual produce of land and labour (and thus public revenue). Measures that reduce production or depress the people's revenue are contrary to the sovereign's interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open markets and freedom of commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereign should 'open the most extensive market for the produce of his country, to allow the most perfect freedom of commerce' and 'abolish, not only all monopolies, but all restraints upon the transportation of the home produce... upon its exportation... or upon the importation of goods of any kind for which it can be exchanged.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate trade measures by their effect on market extent and buyer competition: more buyers and freer movement of goods increase quantity and value of produce and thus sovereign revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving governing power to merchant-interests (conflict of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: When companies of merchants become sovereigns they often continue to 'regard the character of the sovereign as but an appendix to that of the merchant' and make government subservient to mercantile interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies or institutional arrangements that allow commercial motives to dominate sovereign decisions should be criticized for producing actions that favor private profit (monopoly) over public revenue and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration by merchant-councils is prone to despotism and oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'council of merchants' can command obedience only by military force; their government is 'necessarily military and despotical' and tends to make government subservient to monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess governance structures: merchant-dominated administrations are likely to use coercive power to enforce commercial advantage, harming broad public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private trade by company servants creates pervasive monopolies and harms the country
rubrics_metrics.description: The servants of a company trading on their own account will establish monopolies (openly if allowed, secretly if prohibited) and 'tend to reduce the quantity of every sort of produce... and consequently to degrade the cultivation of the whole country, and to reduce the number of its inhabitants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy that permits or fails to check private trading by officials should be judged as likely to produce extractive monopolies, harassment of rivals, suppression of production, and broad social harm. Examples given: forcing peasants to plant opium instead of rice to sell company-held opium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions that drive activity underground are counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting servants from trading 'can have scarce any other effect than to enable its superior servants... to oppress such of the inferior ones' and will lead servants to establish monopolies 'secretly and indirectly' using governmental authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prohibitions not only by intent but by likely behavioral response: if prohibition creates incentives for secret, abusive, or corrupt enforcement, it is worse than transparent private trade and should be avoided or redesigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer long-term public revenue over short-term monopolist profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants 'prefer, upon all ordinary occasions, the little and transitory profit of the monopolist to the great and permanent revenue of the sovereign.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should be scored by whether they enhance sustainable, general revenue (e.g., by increasing production and markets) rather than transient private profits for monopolists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade policy must be evaluated for distributional effects (rich vs poor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mercantile system 'is the industry which is carried on for the benefit of the rich and the powerful... That which is carried on for the benefit of the poor and the indigent is too often either neglected or oppressed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who benefits from trade measures: bounties, duties, or prohibitions that enrich manufacturers and merchants at the expense of poor spinners, labourers, or producers should be judged negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties and duty exemptions should be limited to genuine raw materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemptions and bounties 'are perfectly just and reasonable' when applied to materials of manufacture, but manufacturers have 'extended these exemptions a good deal beyond what can justly be considered as the rude materials of their work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating bounties/exemptions, check if they are narrowly targeted to raw materials (which reduces production costs) or improperly extended to intermediate/finish-stage inputs that mainly increase manufacturers' profits and depress workers' earnings. Examples: foreign brown linen yarn duty reductions and eventual removals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging importation of materials can be defensible if public gain outweighs special-interest capture
rubrics_metrics.description: The importation of materials of manufacture has sometimes been encouraged by exemptions or bounties and 'if, consistently with the necessities of the state, they could be extended to all the other materials of manufacture, the public would certainly be a gainer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such measures should be evaluated on public-interest grounds: do they lower production costs broadly and increase public welfare, or mainly transfer gains to particular manufacturers?

rubrics_metrics.name: Discouraging exportation of materials and instruments to protect manufacturers is harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: The mercantile system 'discourages the exportation of the materials of manufacture, and of the instruments of trade, in order to give our own workmen an advantage' but this often produces oppression and adverse effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess export restrictions by their net economic effect: prohibiting export of raw materials or instruments to protect domestic manufacture often depresses producer incomes and is unjustifiably restrictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe penal restrictions on domestic trade are oppressive and reduce producer welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws restricting inland commerce of wool (marking, packing, time-of-day, reporting requirements, heavy forfeitures and transportation/punishment) are cited as examples of oppressive regulations that reduce price and harm producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate domestic-trade regulations for burdens they impose (penalties, reporting, movement restrictions) and their likely effect to depress prices, reduce production, and harm rural producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy design must account for administrators' incentives and tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: Many company servants 'wish to get out of the country, and consequently to have done with the government, as soon as he can' and consequently act in extractive ways because the country will be indifferent to them once they leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess governance and appointment systems: administrators who are transient and can abscond with fortunes create incentives to extract; policies should seek to align administrators' long-term interests with the country's welfare.
